lead: A sentence is not a flat list of words. Words group into phrases, and phrases into bigger phrases, and a context-free grammar writes those groupings as a small set of rewrite rules: S → NP VP, NP → Det N, VP → V NP. Three sets — nonterminals, terminals and rules — and one start symbol are enough to generate infinitely many sentences, each with its own tree. Parsers, grammar checkers, machine translation decoders and treebank annotators all begin from this object, so it is the first thing syntax in NLP builds.
prereq: You need: word classes and POS tags such as Det, N, V and P from Unit 1 (morphology, word classes) and Unit 2 (POS tagging).

sections.h3: Four sets and a start symbol

blocks.text: A context-free grammar (CFG) is a 4-tuple G = (N, Σ, R, S). N is a finite set of nonterminals: symbols that stand for phrases, written in capitals — S, NP, VP, PP, Det, N, V. Σ is a finite set of terminals: the actual words, written in lower case — the, boy, ate. N and Σ share no symbol. R is a finite set of rules, each written A → β, where A is one nonterminal and β is a string of nonterminals and terminals. S is the start symbol, one member of N; every tree begins there.
Context-free names the left side of a rule: one nonterminal stands alone and is rewritten whatever surrounds it. NP → Det N behaves the same inside the boy ate the cake as at the top of a sentence.

A derivation records the rules applied in order. Write α ⇒ β when one rule turns the string α into β in one step, and S ⇒* w when zero or more steps take S to the terminal string w. A leftmost derivation always rewrites the leftmost nonterminal next. A parse tree shows the same history: root S, each internal node a nonterminal with the children given by the rule used on it, leaves the terminals. The yield of a tree is its leaves read left to right; the tree in the figure has yield “the boy ate a cake”.

Generation asks which strings w satisfy S ⇒* w; that set is the language L(G). Recognition is the reverse: given G and a string w, decide whether w ∈ L(G). A recogniser answers yes or no; a parser returns the trees. How to do it without blind search is in 3.3.
English phrase structure sits in a rule set this small. Nonterminals are capitalised, words are not.

items: S → NP VP — a sentence is a subject noun phrase and a predicate verb phrase.
NP → Det N — a noun phrase is a determiner and a noun.
NP → NP PP — a noun phrase may be a noun phrase plus a prepositional phrase.
VP → V NP — a verb phrase is a verb and its object noun phrase.
VP → VP PP — a verb phrase may take a prepositional phrase.
PP → P NP — a prepositional phrase is a preposition and a noun phrase.
Lexical rules: Det → the | a, N → boy | cake | girl | car | dog | spoon | kitchen, V → ate | saw, P → in | with.

blocks.text: NP → NP PP and PP → P NP feed each other: NP ⇒ NP PP ⇒ NP P NP ⇒ NP PP P NP, so the same six rules produce “the boy with the girl in the car with the dog”. The rule list never grows; only the tree does. This is recursion, and it is why a finite grammar covers unbounded sentences. VP → VP PP does the same on the verb side: “ate the cake with a spoon in the kitchen”.

Some syllabi call these phrase-structure rules, or a phrase-structure grammar (PSG); it is the same object. In the Chomsky hierarchy a CFG is Type 2: it sits above regular grammars (Type 3, finite-state machines from Unit 1) and below context-sensitive grammars (Type 1). The dividing line is counting and nesting: a finite-state machine cannot track how many phrases are still open, a CFG can.

A plain CFG overgenerates. Nothing in S → NP VP blocks “the boys eats”. A feature structure, or attribute-value matrix (AVM), hangs attributes on a symbol: NP becomes [CAT NP, NUM pl, AGR 3pl]. Unification merges two AVMs: it succeeds when no attribute is given two different values, and the result keeps every attribute of both. It fails on [NUM sg] against [NUM pl].

Enforce agreement by requiring the NUM of the subject NP and the NUM of the VP to unify; the value flows from one to the other. “the boys eats” gives NP [NUM pl] and VP [NUM sg], so unification fails and the string is rejected, while “the boy eats” unifies on [NUM sg]. Only a few universities teach feature structures this early; the same machinery returns in unification-based grammars and in feature-based taggers.

spec.aria: A parse tree with S rewritten as NP VP, the first NP as Det N over the boy, the VP as V NP over ate a cake; below, boxes count 6 noun phrases, 12 verb phrases and 72 sentences.

examples.question: Grammar G: S → NP VP; NP → Det N; VP → V NP; Det → the | a; N → boy | cake | girl; V → ate | saw. (a) Give the leftmost derivation of “the boy ate a cake”. (b) How many sentences does G generate?
steps: Start at S, rewrite it by S → NP VP: S ⇒ NP VP.
Leftmost nonterminal is NP; apply NP → Det N: ⇒ Det N VP.
Apply Det → the: ⇒ the N VP.
Apply N → boy: ⇒ the boy VP.
Apply VP → V NP: ⇒ the boy V NP.
Apply V → ate: ⇒ the boy ate NP.
Apply NP → Det N: ⇒ the boy ate Det N.
Apply Det → a: ⇒ the boy ate a N.
Apply N → cake: ⇒ the boy ate a cake. Nine steps, ten strings; the figure draws the parse tree of this derivation.
Count noun phrases: 2 determiners × 3 nouns = 6 NP strings.
Count verb phrases: VP → V NP gives 2 verbs × 6 NP = 12 VP strings.
Count sentences: S → NP VP gives 6 NP × 12 VP = 72 sentences, all of the form Det N V Det N.
examples.answer: The leftmost derivation has nine steps, and G generates 72 sentences.

traps: Writing a terminal as a nonterminal: boy is in Σ and N is in N; the rule is N → boy, never boy → N.
Taking the start symbol to be the first rule written. S is a named member of N; reordering R changes nothing in L(G).
Expecting a plain CFG to enforce agreement. “the boys eats” is generated by an agreement-free rule set; features or a stronger formalism are needed.
Confusing a derivation with a parse tree. The tree forgets step order; one tree can have many derivations but only one leftmost derivation.

quiz.q: Define terminal and nonterminal in a CFG, with one English example of each, and name all four parts of the tuple.
quiz.a: A terminal is a word from Σ, e.g. boy. A nonterminal is a phrase symbol from N, e.g. NP. The tuple is (N, Σ, R, S): nonterminals, terminals, rules, start symbol; N and Σ are disjoint.

quiz.q: Six rules produce unboundedly many sentences. Explain the mechanism.
quiz.a: Recursion. NP → NP PP returns an NP containing a PP, and PP → P NP expands that PP using an NP; repeating adds PPs without adding a rule. VP → VP PP does the same on the verb side.

quiz.q: Using G above, write the leftmost derivation of “the girl saw the boy”.
quiz.a: S ⇒ NP VP ⇒ Det N VP ⇒ the N VP ⇒ the girl VP ⇒ the girl V NP ⇒ the girl saw NP ⇒ the girl saw Det N ⇒ the girl saw the N ⇒ the girl saw the boy. Nine steps.

quiz.q: In G, let Det → the only (one determiner) while N keeps 3 nouns and V keeps 2 verbs. How many sentences does G generate now?
Does G generate “the boy ate the cake in the garden”? Justify, and say what to add.
quiz.a: No. G has no PP rule, no P → in, and no N → garden, so no derivation reaches in the garden. Add PP → P NP, NP → NP PP, VP → VP PP, P → in, and N → garden. Then the PP attaches either to the object NP or to the VP, which is the ambiguity discussed in 3.4.

quiz.q: Why does S → NP VP accept “the boys eats”, and how does unification remove it?
quiz.a: The rule constrains only the category of the two children, not their number. With features, NP carries [NUM pl] and VP carries [NUM sg]; unifying them fails on the NUM attribute, so the tree is rejected. “the boy eats” unifies on [NUM sg].

quiz.q: Where does a CFG sit in the Chomsky hierarchy, and what can it do that a regular grammar cannot?
quiz.a: Type 2, above regular grammars (Type 3). It can express nesting — a phrase inside a phrase inside a phrase — which a finite-state machine cannot track.

beyond: Not for the exam. Real grammar engineering writes rule sets of thousands of rules with feature constraints, and parsers are built over them rather than over the toy grammar here. Search next for unification-based grammars (LFG, HPSG), combinatory categorial grammar, tree adjoining grammar, and the idea of a grammar coupled to a lexicon with valence frames. All of them keep the same core: a finite set of rules, recursion, and a tree per sentence. The step from this chapter to a working system is a treebank, a normal form and a parsing table, which is exactly where the next two chapters go.
